records.rule: newshell objects are made for an LLM to use; a person or a bounded autopilot approves (Tom Dyer, 2026-11-24).
All shell objects extend a common object so ~~table and ~~json work everywhere; a scratch pad keeps references between stages (Tom Dyer, 2026-11-24).
The LLM checks the source of the methods it proposes to use against the object; the source is cached (Tom Dyer, 2026-11-24).
Run proposals using the security manager; it performs the authorisation, e.g. whether ~edit is permitted for the object's path (Tom Dyer, 2026-11-24).
The LLM registers a multi-step plan object; each step has its checks and pass/fail criteria (Tom Dyer, 2026-11-24).
On a message back the LLM is given the job, the stage reached and the stage result, with the error point and trace logs, not the full build output (Tom Dyer, 2026-11-24).
Trigger events such as disk space below n or a log file appearing work the same way (Tom Dyer, 2026-11-24).
A killed step is detected; the LLM reviews the wreckage, plans and executes a cleanup, amends the plan with a fix and runs the new plan (Tom Dyer, 2026-11-24).
Next: put it on ed209g and have Codex drive the work there; start with objects to start an MU and examine networks (Tom Dyer, 2026-11-24).
Codex is its own principal; its plans report to it; Tom's standing rules are deny lines in the cats1 policy (agreed 2026-11-24).
Any order that changes a machine says NEEDS TOM'S DIRECT APPROVAL and never claims Tom approved (standing rule).
Every update states architecture Tom Dyer, who coded, who wrote it, a self-score, signed Claude (Opus 5.5) (standing rule).
